BOW_Note: Rufous-crowned Sparrows also produce calls that function in pair recognition, strengthening of pair bonds, and territorial reinforcement. Chatter Duet and Dear Duet are given between members of a pair while female is building nest and may function to reinforce pair bonds (Wolf 1977). Chatter Duet consists of intense tziit sounds given by male while female produces chatter resembling Alarm Chatter Call (Groschupf 1983). Dear Duet (Figure 4D) consists of a series of dears given in rapid succession by both birds, in which dear notes given by female are shorter, softer, and resemble chatter (Groschupf 1983). Pair Reunion Duet is an uncommon, soft, warbling call performed between members of a pair when they meet within their territory; probably functions to reinforce pair bond. This call resembles “squeal duet” of California Towhees

GS_Note:
Songs of many Apalis species sound very similar, all typically repeating at regular pace a note
or note combination, the latter often showing much variation within a single species. It is
thus not always easy to find species-specific features. Another typical feature is duetting, in
many cases the singing male is joined by the female, either in asynchronous or synchronous
duet. Besides the song and duet, a number of other vocalizations exist, some of which
include elements of the typical song.

BOW_Note: Many (all?) species of Atlapetes have a pair excitement duet; this duet in White-winged is "a liquid descending chatter with some high screeches and twitters"
also a duet, high-pitched and rollicking, with quavering quality that is distinctive.
The pair excitement duet of Cuzco Brush-Finch is "a shrill trill followed by a chatter and tew-tew-tew swee swee?" (Lane, in Schulenberg et al. 2010).
Partners also duet, with much longer song (5–9 seconds) with many stuttering trills and chatters, and less “clean” sound as two birds singing on top of each other and not entirely in synchrony.
chatter-duet a series of nasal thin whistles and slow trills.
also a rambling duet which includes many sweet whistles, trills and more complex notes.

This brushfinch also has a chatter duet (have recording on BOW), described as a "loud, cascading [series] of chipping and twittering notes" (Hilty and Brown 1986) or as a "duet with a lot of buzzy notes, bzt-bzt-bzt, bzbzbzbzbzzbz, speeding up and becoming louder towards [the] end" (Jaramillo 2011).
chatter-duet includes many nasal trills, stutters and chatters.
The pair excitement duet of this brush-finch "includes a characteristic swee tititi chew chew tsew-tsew"

BOW_Note: Duet: Often two birds sing together in duet, but unlike the following two vocal groups, there is apparently not a clear type A and B song, and thus both birds sing a very similar phrase. In Venezuela, there is potential confusion with the very similar-looking Yellow-browed form of Superciliaried Hemispingus (Thlypopsis superciliaris chrysophrys), and claimed different voice in that region ("a pair duetting, one individual giving rapid chatter and the other a series of squeaks and high notes" 24, 25) is more likely voice of the latter taxon.

One bird utters rising song while other bird responds with slow song, presumably members of a pair, the former assumed to be the male and the latter the female, but this requires confirmation. Both song types may be given either alternating or (at least in part) simultaneously.
GS_Note: As noted by Schulenberg et al. (2007), the rising song appears to be given by males and slow song by females, but this is difficult to confirm due to the lack of sexual dichromatism.

BOW_Note: Both sexes produce tonal phrases, with both members of a mated pair often sharing the same phrase types so that they contribute matched phrases to coordinated bouts of song. BOW.Quote: At 25 Vermont nests observed by videography, one female fed at each nest, with two provisioning males most common (60%), followed by nests with one provisioning male (20%), nests with three males (16%), and nests with four males (4%; VCE). Four males documented to feed at >1 nest within single breeding season, and three males fed two broods simultaneously (nests 186–443 m apart). One male simultaneously provisioned at two nests 443 m apart, shared feeding of nestlings at first nest, was sole male feeder at second nest. First nest fledged 3 d after second nest hatched; male then left care of fledglings to the other male and fed second brood at nearly twice the rate as he had fed young at first nest. Individual female, total male, and total adult provisioning rates did not differ between nests with single and multiple male feeders. The number of male feeders was negatively correlated to prey abundance on female home ranges, suggesting that females might balance the cost of low prey abundance by copulating with multiple males and attracting male feeders (Strong et al. 2004). Overall, females fed nestlings at more than twice the rate of males (Goetz et al 2003). Male feeding rates increased with nestling age until day 7–8 and then decreased until fledging. Some males did not feed at nests in which they sired young, and some males fed at nests in which they sired no young (Goetz et al. 2003). Multiple male feeders also reported at nests in Quebec (Y. Aubry) and New Brunswick (Askanas 2012). In highlands of New Brunswick, 78% of nests had two or more male feeders (Askanas 2012). At five nests females provided 57±15% of the feeds at a nest, individual males 21±9%. In Quebec three males attended two different nests in one breeding season (Y. Aubry unpubl.). I

BOW_Note: male and female deliver loudsongs simultaneously in imperfectly synchronized duet.

synchronized duet initiated when female interjects loud buzzy note during male loudsong, at which point male shifts to single buzzy note, lower-pitched than female’s, and the two notes are alternated antiphonally for 3–5 seconds.
female loudsong appears to be regular repetition of its call, a short sharp “zhip”, sometimes given simultaneously with male loudsong but not in clearly synchronized duet.

synchronized duet initiated when female gives slightly higher-pitched doublet at conclusion of male loudsong, at which point male shifts to giving only his doublet, the two doublets then alternated antiphonally.

Male loudsong an introductory note followed by 4–6 doublets with second note lower-pitched; female a short series of usually 4 notes, notes initially longer than those of male but becoming shorter and rising in pitch, usually given in duet after start of male loudsong.

Another vocalization, given by either sex but frequently by both in a syncopated, antiphonal duet, is "a rapidly repeated Chut-up, Chut-up, Chut-up, Chut-up" (Fitzpatrick and Willard 1990). Other calls include "a descending chortling series of musical, hooting whistles: t'hee-hoo-lu'lu'lu'lu'lu" (Lane, in Schulenberg et al. 1990).

femalevideo loudsong similar in all races, a series of countable “wup” notes (e.g. five notes, 1·5 seconds) rising up the scale, notes accelerate slightly or lengthen slightly in some races, often given in duet after start of male loudsong.

Male loudsong 4 or more pairs of notes, each pair consisting of sharp abrupt note followed by longer burry note (e.g. 5 pairs, 2·8 seconds); duet begun when female interjects complex double note into male loudsong, at which point male shifts to single buzzy note, lower-pitched than female’s, and the two notes are alternated.

The song of the female is similar in pattern, but is shorter, higher pitched, and the notes are downslurred (Zimmer and Isler 2003). The song often is given in duet, initiated by the male (Zimmer and Isler 2003).

Male loudsong a series of 4–7 countable (e.g. 4 notes, 1·5 seconds) sharp notes rising in pitch and accelerating slightly; female similar but lower-pitched and often followed by 2–4 soft abrupt notes, usually given in duet at end of male loudsong.

BOW.Quote: Although White-rumped Shama is not reported to be a cooperative breeding species, helping behavior was observed at 2 out of 32 nests on O‘ahu I. (8). In each case, 2 different adult males were observed feeding nestlings of a single female. At one of these nests, 2 males fed the single nestling at 1, 9, 10, and 12 d after hatching; the males did not behave aggressively toward one another. At the other nest, a second male was observed on a single day; it fed the nestlings 3 times but was attacked repeatedly by resident male. Unknown whether these males were reproductively inactive helpers, or if they sired some of the nestlings through extra-pair copulations or polyandrous matings.

BOW_Note: Song of two types, territorial in function, often given antiphonally by pairs. First type (probably by male) a clear, hurried “chwi-pieu”, “pi-pweu” or “wiwi-weu”, repeated every few seconds, alternatively as thin, sweet, quick, anxious-sounding whistle with short downslurred and then upslurred introductory note, “tui’téééér” (“ééé” strongly downslurred and ending abruptly at low point), or longer version with more and higher-pitched introductory notes. Second type (probably by female) a loud staccato rattling trill, usually with shorter introductory note, “cho-prrrrrrt” or “chrrru-prrrrrrt”, repeated after slightly longer intervals.

Song a loud, quite high-pitched, rising whistleaudio repeated every 3–5 seconds, typically “wueeeeoo” or “u-weeeeoo” (rising in middle), “uuuu-weeoo” (rising more at start), “wiu-weeeu” (quick first note, stressed second note), or “wu-eeyou” (rising sharply at end); variants include “weeoo-wiu”, “yiuuuu-ee”, “wuuuu-ip” and “wuuuu-oo” (last two heard in duet), sometimes a shorter “u-weeaa”.

BOW.Quote: Females only incubate and brood the young, but both males and females bring food to the nestlings. Group members help during nesting. During nest building, group members only follow the nest building female around the territory, although Willis (1961) observed one non-reproductive individual carrying material to the nest. Helpers contribute with nest defense and feeding nestlings; helpers start feeding nestlings on day 5 after hatching and, on average, they make 4.5% (18 of the 397) of the total feeding trips (Willis 1961).

BOW_Note: Song, by pair, trio or quartet (occasionally quintet) of foraging birds in early morning, more or less simultaneously by group-members at intervals of c. 15 seconds: one individual (same one each time?) starts, others immediately join in with identical songs sounding slightly out of sync, producing vibrating chorus lasting c. 5 seconds, each bird singing chattery stream of high-pitched “chipa’chipa’ chip-chit’chit’chit’chit’it’it’it...”, accelerating, then slowing.

In SE Peru (Cuzco, 1500 m) at dawn, individuals (race berlepschi) sing duets, trios or quartets of high, fast, tinkling “tsink’a’lee, tsink’a’lee, tsink’a’lee... ti, ti..ti”, typically 5–6 “tsink’a’lee” phrases in almost explosive burst, then dying away and ending with irregular “ti” notes for few seconds, before song abruptly restarted by pair or group, song bout often continuing for several minutes.

Song (races maculifrons and leucogastrus) primarily just after dawn, often as duet, trio or quartet, bursts 3–4 seconds long of rapid high notes, rather dry and harsh, that accelerate and become louder (cadence reminiscent of ocean waves rolling onshore), may be repeated at short intervals.

Song, singly or in duets or trios, a burst 5–15 seconds long of squeaky twittering notes mixed with stream of higher-pitched thin “seet” or “steet” notes; squeaky notes may cease for intervals of 10–12 seconds before another song initiated, but very high “seet” notes may continue at slower rate.

BOW.Quote: Nests often attract the attention of extra adults that associate with a pair for up to an entire breeding season; these extra birds are sometimes tolerated and occasionally lead to polygyny (217). In New York, extra birds were predominantly males (219, 325), whereas in Washington, extra birds were yearling females (217). Extra adults contribute relatively little to feeding young, but they are known to mob predators and assist in nest-building, incubation, and brooding young (219, 325, 217). Extra adults may be using nest attendance as a breeding strategy either to replace one pair member should something happen to it (217) or to commit sexually selected infanticide (219, 325), providing an opportunity for males to take over the breeding female (see Behavior: Sexual Behavior). Nests that are attended by helpers often are ones occupied by older females (325), consistent with the interpretation that male attendants are trying to secure high-quality females as mates.

Pair utters precisely synchronized callsvideo in duet. Commonest duet a loud, pure, resonant, liquid double "whee-u" or "kweeho" or "tyaw" whistle by one individual, partner giving dry rasping rattle or short trill of 2–4 clicks, "kikiki" or "ch-chacha", duet lasts 0·3–0·4 seconds; male and female motifs each 0·2–0·3 seconds and overlap, with auditory response time of 0·08–0·1 seconds. Male usually initiates duet with "whee-u" but female can do so with "kikiki"; apparently each sex can both whistle and rattle; some duets tripartite, "huweeu-kkkk-huweeu". Single bird commonly utters repeated rhythmic "twoo-woo" whistle. Eight pairs used eight different duet patterns, and any one pair uses several different forms of "whee-u" call. One type of duet is repeated 10–40 times, with very regular intervals of 1·16–1·70 seconds between duets, then, after pause of several seconds, pair sings series of another duet type.
Ref: Payne, R. B. "Duetting and chorus singing in African birds." Ostrich 42.S1 (1971): 125-146.

BOW_Note: Some calls rendered as loud high “kee kee…”, hoarse “que que…”, loud “whit whit…”, soft “cremm”, loud clear “pip pip…”, and “kee qui qui…”. Duets; on Mt Albert Edward, two individuals faced each other on a branch and uttered “caw” notes rapidly and in perfect alternation up to 34 times.

Noisy. Vocalizations often comprise 4–5 nasal slurs; also loud, descending “whee oo wooo”, and bell-like notes like those of Blue Bird-of-paradise (Paradisornis rudolphi). Often duets, giving nasal slurs in perfect alternating rhythm.
Ref: Diamond, Jared M. "Further examples of dual singing by southwest Pacific birds." The Auk 89.1 (1972): 180-183.

BOW.Quote: Although ca. 20% of Canada Jay pairs studied in Quebec and Ontario have an associated nonbreeder on their territories at the onset of breeding and ca. 65% of these are the pair's own offspring from the previous breeding season, the nonbreeders do not feed the current year's nestlings and the breeders energetically drive them away if they approach the nest. Starting immediately after the nestlings fledge, however, adults relax this vigilance and on intensively observed territories in Ontario and Quebec some non-breeders have accounted for over 30% of all observed feedings of the young (189, 190). Proposed explanation for this pattern holds that, compared to other jays, Canada Jays are particularly vulnerable to nest predators because they have poorer defensive abilities (being smaller and generally having only one extra group member, if any). In such a species, suppression of allofeeding, along with a smaller than expected clutch size and a very low provisioning rate by the adults (achieved by bringing largest possible loads at the consequently minimum possible frequency), may reduce predator-attracting visits to the nest and thus contribute to higher breeding success (166, 191). Strickland, D. and T. A. Waite. (2001). Does initial suppression of allofeeding in small jays help to conceal their nests? Canadian Journal of Zoology 79 (12):2128-2146. Strickland, D. (2003). BOW_Note: Song a series of loud ringing notesvideo introduced by 1–2 softer notes, “ku, keeé-keeé-keeé-keeé-keeé-kuh”. Compared to that of P. erythrophthalmus, song is lower-pitched (mean 2·84 kHz vs. 3·95 kHz), briefer (lasting less than c. 2 seconds on average, whereas P. erythrophthalmus lasts > 3 seconds) and comprises fewer notes (on average 5·15 as opposed to 6·17), and is usually given from just 1 m above ground or water. Duets last longer in both species, on average almost 11 seconds in present species though again longer in P. erythrophthalmus (more than 13·5 seconds), with more notes (in this case, the present species gives more notes, > 23 on average, vs. > 21 notes) but remains lower-pitched.

Other_FemaleSong: "Babble-Singing, Soft Singing, Whisper Song, and Rhythmic Singing. Often accompanied by raised head and flashing of white nictitating membrane; usually uttered only by males. Probably the equivalent of song in other passerines; can be heard from only about 50 m (Baeyens 1979a). Dominant Black-billed Magpies often approach predator, or even human intruder, and challenge it by Babble-Singing in self-assertive manner; described as ‚Äúcheeky‚Äù behavior by Birkhead (Birkhead 1991), when directed toward him. Often starts with soft chatters of 1 or 2 notes; then gradually progresses into whistled subsong of 6‚Äì7 syllables. For a sonogram of this and several other calls, see Birkhead 1991: 68. This challenging or assertive behavior given around predators has never been observed in European magpies (Birkhead 1991). Soft Singing is uttered quietly, usually by courting males; similar Whisper Song is given by both sexes during nest-building (Cramp and Perrins 1994a). Louder Rhythmic Singing also given by males during courtship. Both Soft Singing and Rhythmic Singing sound like subsongs. Rhythmic Singing seems more rigid in sequence and stereotyped than Babble-Singing. Babble-Singing is often given by young, aggressive males, but a wild adult female was heard to give this varied whistlelike song while sitting alone in a flight cage (CHT), and young magpies between 6 and 20 wk old have been heard uttering this call (Cramp and Perrins 1994a). "

BOW_Note: Mate-Call (Squeal Duet, Duet Squeal or “pair reunion duet” of Marshall [Marshall 1964c: 349]). Squeal-churrrr or squeal—squeal-squeal-squeal; “exactly the same as that of [Canyon Towhee]”; readily told in field from laughing squeal-cha-cha-cha or squeal-hah-hah-hah of Abert's Towhee (Marshall and Johnson 1968: 629). Series of squeaking sounds, similar to that made with person's lips (RRJ). Squeal duets may begin when partners are physically separated, but do not end until mates are within a meter of each other. Squeal vocalizations are generally constructed of three syllable types: an introductory squeak, a descending frequency sweep and a broadband squeal. Individuals vary the numbers of each note type in each squeal vocalization, but always produce the three syllables in the order listed. Roughly 95% of squeal vocalizations are given as part of duets (Benedict and McEntee 2009). Squeal duets are sometimes accompanied by displays that include fluttering of the partners' wings and opening of the bills (LB, RRJ)
Ref: Marshall, Joe T. "Voice in communication and relationships among brown towhees." The Condor 66.5 (1964): 345-356.

Flock-members and pair-members keep in touch by mellow bubbling or gurgling calls and song duets, the combined sound seeming to be given by one bird.
Song a geographically and individually variable series of usually 3 short, syncopated, loud, hollow notes, the higher notes sweet and sad-sounding, often from duetting pairs,

Commonly sings  in duet, very like E. erythrogenys, a quick, loud, far-carrying fluty 2-note phrase answered by very short sharp note, e.g. “wi-wru-pi…”, “wip-uip-ju…” or “wi-wu-jrr…”; also described as quick, syncopated, clear “kwíhdu”, first note strident, second weak and mellow, often with higher, slightly falling “péék” note or, less often, harsher, burry downslurred “brréér” by second bird; also quick staccato “kerwíck!”, second note upturned, or similar “kérwérk!”, second note only slightly higher.

Vocalizations differ distinctly from those of P. horsfieldii, being higher-pitched, with more melodious and less hollow-sounding notes; an “oop-oop-oop-oop…” and sonorous, pleasant “pawp-a-pawp” answered presumably by female with “kaa-kree, kaa-kree”; also descending “do do do do do”, “pop pop-prrr” and deep “woch wohorro”.

Songvideo variable, including rather husky “wuh-wuh-wuh-wree”, repeated every 5–9 seconds, quickly answered by jollier “wu-wii” (second note rising), also a hollow piping “uh-pu-pu-pu” (sometimes more hurried “wup’u’wu”) answered by low harsh husky “whéér-wu’wu”.

BOW.Quote: Polygynandrous mating system, 2–5 males share large overlapping ranges of 2–5 females, group ranges (9–38 ha) more or less exclusive; males compete to mate with fertile females, females compete to attract males; solicitation display by female, which has high copulation rate (up to 1000 per clutch), usually involving several males. Five breeding groups studied in a Swiss alpine region each consisted of 1–4 females with exclusive territories, and 3–5 males which co-operated in defending group territory; within group, linear dominance relationship usually well established among alpha, beta and subordinate males, both frequent copulation and mate-guarding strategies being used, and females advertised their fertility, solicited most of copulations and mated many times with several males (c. 350 matings during short fertile period of ten days), while intensity of mate-guarding and copulation frequency were highest on day preceding and throughout laying period; in this polygynandrous system, females of studied population lacked full male help but might have benefited from greater genetic variation of their offspring, while males varied widely in lifetime reproductive success, higher-ranking males raising their fitness to above average (4). Nest, built by female, a cup made from grass, moss and plant stems, lined with hair and feathers, sited in rock crevice or beneath rock or grass tussock on cliff or shallower slope. Clutch 3–4 eggs; incubation by female, period 11–15 days; chicksphoto fed by both sexes, but contribution of each male varies; of 38 broods studied in Pyrenees, 5% fed by female alone, 68% by female and one male, 24% by female and two males, 3% by female and three males; male care influenced by share of matings, hence paternity

BOW_Note: Antiphonal singing noted, and territorial calls reportedly carry farther. When nesting, female may leave nest and call, male answering quickly and then appearing with food. Mimicry reported but not in full song, some calls similar to those of whipbird (Psophodes).Alarm a trisyllabic “witwit-wong” and disyllabic “wit-tui”, used when partners separated; if no response to this, song may be given; disyllabic “teewit” usually given by female in reply to male’s song. Single upward-inflected “see” when male offers food to female or when feeding young. Fledglings give soft wheezing call when following parents and give quiet songs after c. 2 months.

BOW.Quote: In contrast to Western Bluebirds, Eastern Bluebirds rarely have helpers. In joint nesting, 2 females lay 2 clutches of eggs synchronously in the same nest, then incubate synchronously and sequentially, and cooperate with a male in feeding nestlings and fledglings. In S. Carolina, 5 of 4,299 nesting attempts in field seasons 1977‚Äì1991 were joint nesting ventures; 2 of these 5 attempts were by the same previously known and banded females, so it was reliably inferred that these jointly-nesting females were mother and daughter (PAG, JHP). Juvenile helpers are rare; almost all reports are of juveniles entering nesting cavities when adults are feeding later broods (Pinkowski 1975d)‚Äîsomething documented on video films twice by PAG and JHP. Adult helpers seen occasionally and irregularly (Pinkowski 1976d, PAG), usually second-year son of current breeders.

BOW.Quote: Extremely rare if not absent in most temperate populations. One report from California of a juvenile from a first brood helping its father (and possibly mother; she was unmarked) feed young of a second brood in the same season (275. Second report from Kansas of a juvenile of unknown origin feeding young and removing a fecal sac from a nest at least one time (Timson and Farley 2003). Helpers-at-the-nest also reported in Costa Rica, but not in all nests and such behavior was apparently rare (Skutch 1940, 176, Skutch 1983, Winnett-Murray 1986). Skutch (1983) speculated helping was more likely when young from a previous brood sleep with the mother in the nest while she incubates in a subsequent breeding attempt. In one case in Costa Rica, an individual known not to be the offspring of a resident parents' previous brood attempted to feed young; parents repeatedly attacked that individual (Winnett-Murray 1986: 23).

Trios of adults occasionally form, but are rarely stable; a trio in New York remained together from early in nestling period to > 1 mo after young had fledged (MTM). The fate of the third bird in next year was determined in 2 of 3 cases in which the third bird was banded and sex determined. In one case, a female returned to breed on territory where she was seen in previous year (former male and female occupants of territory failed to return). In the other case, a male established residence on adjacent territory in following year. Third birds in trios probably represent birds prospecting for a breeding site in the next year. BOW_Note: Not noisy, but commonly heard throughout day. Main call a series of rather loud single whistles, rising and falling in pitch and loudness; in E New Guinea, consists of a phrase of usually 3 (sometimes 2) notes, “whit-wut-wu” or “whip-to-whee” (length of phrases 1–1·6 seconds), repeated 3–10 or more times (at rate of c. 6·5–7·5 phrases per 10 seconds); some variation in calls, with one to all notes in phrase disyllabic, or phrase sometimes incomplete; also some apparent geographical variation in phrases and speed of delivery. Antiphonal duets reported. In New Guinea, contact call an excited “tip-tip-tip-tip-tip”, given in flight or during foraging in mixed-species flocks, and when disturbed gives high-pitched “tjiewiet-tiet…tjiewiet-tiet” (a characteristic call of forests where it occurs).
